findings.title: F25 / F26 FY2023-24 do not use F14's capitalisation

findings.title: Receivables: the Commission and the petitioner use different bases
findings.detail: NPCL's projection takes 1.5 months of tariff and open-access revenue; the Commission's FY2025-26 approval (as F27 restates it) takes tariff revenue alone (370.25 × 12 / 1.5 = 2,962.0).  True-up years use billing (FY2022-23 grossed up by 1.0473).

findings.title: F18 prints its ARR column as FY 2025-26

findings.title: Carrying cost on a surplus: full rate (Commission) or 75 % of a deposit rate (NPCL)
findings.detail: The Commission's approvals, as NPCL restates them, carry a surplus at the full carrying rate (FY2024-25: × 11.05 %, Rs 122.34 crore); NPCL's own columns at 75 % of a deposit rate (6.75 %; 6.5 % for FY2026-27) — Rs 56.05 crore for the same base.

findings.title: Depreciation: land on a base excluding land rights; one office-equipment year
findings.detail: NPCL depreciates land at 3.34 % of the average gross block less the non-depreciable land rights (3.99); FY2024-25 office equipment (pre-2020 assets) is 0.5373 where the class rate gives 0.5073.

findings.title: F24 FY2023-24: the rate column divides by the net block
findings.detail: The FY2023-24 block's "Applicable rate" (J38:J56) is G / ((B − F) + (C − D) / 2) — the year's depreciation over the opening gross block less accumulated depreciation; the FY2024-25 to FY2026-27 blocks divide by the gross block (B + (C − D) / 2), and FY2022-23 prints the rate itself.  Land therefore shows 3.67 % in FY2023-24 against 3.34 % in the other years.  The depreciation figures are unaffected; the printed rates are not comparable across years.

findings.title: Depreciation of the APR and ARR years: the computation is not in the filing
findings.detail: F24 types each class's depreciation for FY2025-26 and FY2026-27.  Annexure-21 rolls only the existing assets forward (gross 111.39 for FY2025-26 against F24's 121.04).  The excess fits half a year at the class rate on the year's additions for land, buildings, vehicles and metering (0.50), but about 0.40 for lines & cables, plant & machinery and communication equipment in FY2025-26, and no single fraction in FY2026-27.  Consumer-contribution depreciation is 30.94 in F24 against 29.65 in the workings.  The totals reproduce from F24's class figures (net 90.09 and 106.75, as the ARR carries); the class figures themselves cannot be derived from what was filed.  Ask for the working, e.g. additions by month or by funding source.

findings.title: Interest on security deposit, FY2024-25: March typed, not computed
findings.detail: F30 computes each month's interest as the month's average deposit × 6.75 % / 12; March (M10) is typed as 1.8901 where the formula gives 2.0802.  The year's total is therefore 24.79 (carried to F30A, F25 row 16 and the ARR's row 38) where the monthly balances give 24.98.  The claim is 0.19 below the computation — it reads as the interest actually disbursed with March as the balancing month; the petitioner should say so, and the reviewer should allow the amount disbursed, not the computation.  Carried end to end (increment 95: each year's opening fed from the year before as computed), the 0.19 travels with carrying cost into the regulatory asset: FY2024-25 closes at (267.94) against the filed (267.74), FY2025-26 at (629.59) against (629.37), and FY2026-27 at (1,002.64) against (1,002.39) — 0.25 crore of the gap carried forward rests on how March is treated.

findings.title: ESR-3 FY2024-25: a typed 0.04 in the regulatory-discount total

So the discount column and the revenue total disagree by Rs 0.04 crore; the revenue the ARR carries (2,634.60) is the rows' sum.  The petitioner should say what the 0.04 is.

findings.title: Urban domestic revenue implies rates 1.8–1.9 % below the schedule in force

findings.title: Power purchase: the claim is 1.50 below the reconciliation with the audited accounts
findings.detail: Annexure-14 bridges the audited accounts (Note 46(b): net charges 2,093.62, transmission 294.40) to the true-up claim: less 36.94 booked in FY2024-25 but claimed in another year, plus 120.46 of earlier years' claims = 2,471.54.  PPC FY 25 claims 2,470.04 (the ARR's rows 20 + 22 + 23).  The 1.50 is the carrying cost for FY2023-24: 12.88 in the reconciliation, 11.37 in PPC FY 25 (row 77).  The split between the year's sources and the arrears also differs by 8.77 — the 10 % of FY2022-23 and FY2023-24 additional coal booked in FY2024-25, inside the accounts' base in the annexure and among the arrears in PPC — which nets to nothing.  Which carrying cost is right?

findings.title: BS1 (profit and loss) is built from the ARR format, not taken from the audited accounts
findings.detail: Every figure of BS1 is a formula over the ARR format (revenue = ARR row 17, power purchase = rows 20–24, employee = row 29, finance costs = rows 37–40 and 45 less 62, depreciation = row 36, tax = row 44) or over F22 / F23.  It restates the claim as a profit and loss account; it is not evidence that the claim agrees with the audited accounts.  The reviewer should reconcile the true-up year to the audited accounts (Annexure-1(a)) and the trial balance (Annexure-41) themselves.  Annexure-14 does so for power purchase only (A44).

findings.title: Employee expenses claimed exceed the trial balance by exactly Rs 0.0105 crore
findings.detail: The trial balance's employee benefits expense (Note 30, 19 accounts before capitalisation) is 95.409346859 crore; F21 claims 95.419846859 — exactly 0.0105 crore (Rs 1.05 lakh) more, every other digit equal, so one typed component differs by that amount.  Capitalisation agrees (17.19), so net employee expenses (the ARR's row 29) are 78.23 claimed against 78.22 in the books.  Everything else checked against the trial balance agrees to the paisa of a crore: power purchase and transmission net of rebate, interest on security deposit (24.79, which supports A40's reading), finance charges, bad debts written off, loss on retired assets.  Which F21 line carries the 0.0105?

findings.title: F32: the ARR summary column double-counts interest; the allocation base is not the net ARR
findings.detail: F32's 'ARR summary' column (L) adds the net interest line (L16 = ARR rows 37–40, 119.31) and also its parts (L17, L18): its ARR is 3,692.18 where the allocated columns give 3,572.87 — 119.31 counted twice.  Only the allocated columns (F, H) feed the cross-subsidy surcharge (F33), so the double count does not reach it.  The allocated base itself is not the net ARR (3,481.83): it adds the regulatory assets' carrying cost (83.23, F33's R), leaves out provisions (3.00) and does not deduct other-business income and open-access revenue (10.82).  The reviewer should decide the base the cost of supply for the surcharge is computed on.

findings.title: RPO: losses and sales not the filing's own; obligations netted across categories
findings.detail: F6 brings renewable purchases to the distribution periphery with transmission losses typed into its formulas: 3.58 % inter-state and 3.18 % intra-state for FY2025-26 and FY2026-27, where the Energy Balance has 3.55 % / 3.30 % (FY2025-26) and 3.41 % / 3.35 % (FY2026-27); for FY2024-25 3.46875 % / 3.20862 % against 3.46868 % / 3.21055 %.  Its sales differ from ESR-3 by about 0.004 MU each year (3,597.6329 against 3,597.6293 for FY2024-25).  The year's obligation adds the solar, non-solar and hydro balances, so a surplus in one category (FY2026-27 solar −154.32 MU, non-solar −134.81 MU) offsets a shortfall in another (hydro +141.88 MU), and a net surplus (−147.25 MU) is carried forward as a credit.  FY2025-26's REC purchase is typed equal to that year's obligation (215.12 MU).  The reviewer should decide whether categories are fungible and whether a surplus carries forward; the petitioner should use the Energy Balance's losses.

findings.title: Distribution loss: P1_DL claims more than the petition is computed at
findings.detail: P1_DL's 'Claimed' column gives 7.45 % for FY2025-26 and 7.42 % for FY2026-27 (and 7.40 %, 7.38 %, 7.37 % for the next control period, against the Commission's 6.70 %, 6.43 %, 6.16 %).  The Energy Balance and the ARR format — and so the power purchase, sales and ARR — use 7.23 % and 6.97 %, the Commission's approved losses.  For FY2024-25 P1_DL's 7.479277 % differs from the Energy Balance's 7.479214 % in the sixth decimal.  Which loss does NPCL claim?  If it claims P1_DL's, the energy requirement and the power purchase of the APR and ARR years are understated; if the approved, P1_DL should say so.

findings.title: Cross-subsidy surcharge capped at 20 % of the ABR, where the 2025 Regulations say 20 % of the average cost of supply
findings.detail: The candidate clause (MYT Distribution Regulations 2025, p.48) reads: 'the Cross Subsidy Surcharge shall not exceed 20% of the Average Cost of Supply'.  F33 caps at 20 % of each category's average billing rate (G107 = MIN(20 % × D107, F107)), although its own column header says 'with a cap of 20% of ACoS'; the draft rule uperc.oa.css follows F33.  At ACoS 7.91 Rs/kWh the cap would be 1.58; the surcharges computed for FY2026-27 (1.21) are below either cap, so the figures do not change this year — the rule does.  The reviewer should verify the clause and amend the draft rule.

findings.title: Bad and doubtful debts capped at 2 % of receivables, where the 2025 Regulations say 2 % of revenue from the sale of electricity in the audited accounts
findings.detail: The candidate clause (MYT Distribution Regulations 2025, p.45) allows 'a provision for write-off of bad and doubtful debts up to the extent of 2% of revenue from the sale of electricity as reflected in the audited accounts'.  P3 (and the draft rule uperc.baddebts.cap) takes 2 % of 'receivables for the year', which F31 builds as receipts × 1.0532.  NPCL's claims (12.44, 13.76) are far below either cap, so nothing changes this year; the base of the cap should follow the clause once verified.

findings.title: Urban domestic energy charges filed 1.8–1.9 % below units sold × the schedule's slab rates (Rs. 9.87 crore in FY2026-27)
findings.detail: Computed from the units sold (ESR-3 column F) and the energy rates of the order's Annexure-I (page 365: 5.50, 5.50, 6.00, 6.50 Rs/kWh), the four 'Domestic Other Metered' slabs give 110.7788, 43.4680, 98.5036 and 294.6805 crore; ESR-3 files 108.6854, 42.6614, 96.7187 and 289.4981 (ratios 0.9811, 0.9814, 0.9819, 0.9824), 9.8673 crore less in all.  The regulatory discount is a separate column (N), so it is not the cause.  The pattern is consistent with the 2 % discount on the 'RATE' for consumers with prepaid meters (Annexure-I, General Provisions 11(i), page 357) applied to about 88–95 % of each slab's sales — a reading, not a fact.  The other 40 slabs bound (rural domestic, LMV-2, LMV-4, LMV-5, LMV-6 with its time-of-day rates, LMV-11) reproduce exactly from the same schedule.  The petitioner should state the basis: the prepaid share by slab, or the other adjustment applied.  The rates are those ESR-3 is at: the existing rates NPCL states in ESR4A (column C, rows 34–37) are these same rates, as are all 47 existing energy rates it states (increment 92).
where: ESR_3 Curr Tariff FY27 rows 23–26 (F, K)

findings.title: Registered societies (single-point bulk supply) filed at 6.3465 Rs/kWh against the schedule's 7.00 (Rs. 40.21 crore less in FY2026-27)
findings.detail: Units sold 615.3353 MU (ESR-3 F20) at the order's bulk-supply energy rate of Rs. 7.00/kWh (Annexure-I, page 363) give 430.7347 crore of energy charges; ESR-3 files 390.5230 (K20), 9.34 % less.  The order converts kWh rates to kVAh rates by the factor 0.90 for consumers billed in kVAh (Annexure-I, General Provisions 5, page 353), which gives Rs. 6.30/kVAh; the filed figure equals 6.30 × 1.0074 per kWh — consistent with kVAh billing if the kVAh sold exceed the kWh shown by 0.74 %, but ESR-3 shows kWh only, so that is a reading, not a fact.  The petitioner should state the kVAh sold to this category and the rate applied.

findings.title: HV energy charges are billed per kVAh but ESR-3 states only kWh sold, so HV revenue (1,740.21 crore of energy charges in FY2026-27, ESR-3 K92:K135) cannot be recomputed from the filing
findings.detail: The order prices HV-1 to HV-4 per kVAh (Annexure-I pp.384–393; HV-1 at 11 kV Rs. 8.32/kVAh, HV-2 up to 11 kV Rs. 7.10/kVAh), and NPCL's ESR4A states the same existing rates.  ESR-3's HV rows give units sold in MU (kWh) and energy charges, so the energy charges divided by the kVAh rate (with the HV-2 time-of-day percentages, p.388) imply the kVAh billed per kWh sold: HV-1 commercial 1.0348 at 11 kV and 1.0119 above; HV-1 public 1.0409 and 1.0279; HV-2 1.0428–1.0458 up to 11 kV, 1.0175–1.0203 at 11–66 kV, 1.0274–1.0341 at 66–132 kV — power factors of 0.96 to 0.99, plausible, but derived from the answer, not from a stated quantity.  The engine refuses to multiply a kVAh rate by kWh (they are different units).  The petitioner should state the kVAh sold by HV category and voltage (and time-of-day slot), so the HV revenue can be computed from the rates.
where: ESR_3 Curr Tariff FY27 rows 92–135 (F, K)

findings.title: Reg. 6.4 requires the true-up's accounts under the Accounts and Additional Disclosure Rules 2024 and amendments; NPCL states it will comply with the Rules from FY2026-27
findings.detail: The 2025 Regulations (Reg. 6.4, p.12): 'The Distribution Licensee shall ensure that its Accounting Statements are prepared in compliance of the Electricity Distribution (Accounts and Additional Disclosure) Rules, 2024 and any amendment thereof.'  NPCL's compliance report (Appendix VII, against the directives of the order of 22.11.2025) answers 'Being Complied' for the detailed break-ups in the FY2024-25 audited accounts (power purchase by source, transmission losses and charges, category-wise billing determinants and revenue), and adds that the Rules as notified on 25 September 2025 come into effect from 01.04.2026, 'Accordingly, the Company will ensure compliance with the said Rules from FY 2026-27 onwards.'  Whether the FY2024-25 accounts meet Reg. 6.4 — the 2024 Rules, or only the disclosures the Commission named — is for the reviewer with the audited accounts (Annexure-1(a)) in hand.  Found by the filing checklist (U25-6.4).

findings.title: The Commission's O&M approval for FY2026-27 reproduces with the same draft rules as NPCL's claim; the 18.37 cut is a refused growth factor (11.62), three inflation averages (1.10), the approved GFA base and GNIDA (2.65) and the provision (3.00)

For the next petition: support any growth factor with the benchmarking report; escalate the ARR year by the three-year average; take the GFA split the Commission approved.

findings.title: The order's ARR summary (Table 6-81) prints approved interest charges of 110.80 where its interest table (6-72) approves 110.43; the summary's own ARR (3,420.27) adds up only with 110.43
findings.detail: Table 6-72 (p.286) approves interest on long-term loans 85.60, on working capital nil, on security deposits 20.51 and banking and finance charges 4.32: 110.43.  Table 6-81 (p.294) prints 'Interest Charges … 110.80' in the approved column; its lines then add to 3,420.65, but it prints the Annual Revenue Requirement as 3,420.27 — the sum with 110.43 (3,420.28, rounding) — and the net ARR (3,511.33) and gap (319.29) follow from 3,420.27.  The approved totals are therefore consistent with 110.43 and the 110.80 line reads as a misprint (found by the order's own arithmetic, now checked per column: every other column of the three summary tables adds up).  Similarly, Table 6-50 (p.258) gives the claimed total O&M as 245.92 where the summary's gross O&M is 242.92 (the former includes the 3.00 provision).  For the reviewer — and for the petitioner, should it seek a correction.

findings.title: The capital and interest approvals for FY2026-27 reproduce with the same rules; RoE −2.49, interest −8.88, tax −0.84 and depreciation −2.95 trace to the approved opening balances, the disallowed capex and two rates
findings.detail: Fed the order's figures (Tables 6-58, 6-67, 6-70, 6-72, 6-74, 6-76), the capital, MYT 2025 and tax rules give the Commission's funding (to fund 409.84, debt 286.89, equity 122.95, deletions 2.18 and 4.50), normative loan (closing 961.61, interest 85.60 — at NPCL's own rate, which the order accepts, para 6.10.5), equity (closing 814.43, RoE 113.28), tax 38.10 and security-deposit interest 20.51 (bindings/approval-capital-fy27.json, 13 / 14; the average equity is 755.21 against the printed 755.20, the order's opening equity being itself rounded).  Against NPCL's claim: RoE −2.49 = the opening equity approved in the APR (695.98 against 709.62: −2.05) and 30 % of the 19.56 of capex disallowed — metering/AMI 15.56 and cyber resilience 4.00 (−0.44); interest −8.88 = interest on the normative loan +1.72 (the approved opening loan 780.70 against 757.77 outweighs the lower additions), security deposit −3.73 (5.50 % allowed against 6.50 %), working capital −6.88 (the surplus of 73.34 at the beginning of the year leaves no working capital to fund); tax −0.84 follows RoE.  For the next petition: take the opening balances the Commission approved, and the deposit rate it allows.  Depreciation −2.95 (increment 99, bindings/approval-depreciation-fy27.json: every class's depreciation reproduces; closings and part totals within two units of the last place, the order printing its GFA rounded): Part A −2.91 (assets up to 31.03.2020 on the approved opening GFA of 1,062.12 — NPCL's FAR basis is 1,148.63), Part B −0.26, Part C +0.21 (the full 474.13 of approved additions, against the 462.82 NPCL's depreciation working used, para 6.8.7).

findings.title: The order's power purchase table (6-35) prints NPCL's claimed short-term total as 810.23 where the petition has 810.53 and the order's own rows add to 810.52; and the claimed JITPL rate as 5.62 where its amount implies 5.61

Neither touches the approval.  For the reviewer.

findings.title: Power purchase +29.04 and transmission +35.13 for FY2026-27: DIL priced at its trued-up tariff, the short-term mix replaced by the contracts the Commission approved and the exchange, the surplus sale and DSM not allowed, UPPTCL at its own tariff order
findings.detail: From Table 6-35 read by position (51 rows, the approved side's arithmetic 100 %): long-term DIL +46.35 — the same 1,188.64 MU at a landed 4.89 Rs/kWh against 4.50, the Commission taking DIL's normative auxiliary consumption and ex-bus fixed and energy charges for FY2023-24 from its true-up order of 20.03.2026 (para 6.5.38, Table 6-26); short-term −79.14 — NPCL's trader and exchange blocks (1,246.64 MU) replaced by the short-term agreements the Commission approved in its orders on Petitions 2341/2025 and 2339/2025 (751.49 MU with TPTCL's, Table 6-33) and 617.63 MU from the exchange at 4.67 Rs/kWh, the fourteen-month IEX DAM average (para 6.5.51) — 576.59 MU at NPCL's periphery after the ISTS 3.58 % and intra-state 3.18 % losses, so the table's 5.00 Rs/kWh is per periphery unit; renewable −0.32 (APPCPL's LT solar not approved); the sale at IEX (−59.72) and DSM (−2.44) not allowed, to be settled at true-up (paras 6.5.52–6.5.53): +62.16.  Transmission: UPPTCL 223.88 against 188.50 (+35.38) at UPPTCL's own tariff order (para 6.5.55), SLDC −0.25.  For the next petition: price DIL at the trued-up tariff, plan short-term purchases from approved agreements, and leave the surplus sale and DSM to true-up.
